amendments.rule: A repeated or resumptive element that the ASV renders once is still its own unit. Mark the unrepresented occurrence `unrepresented` rather than folding it into the rendered one. Where the repetition is a counted noun distributed across a compound numeral — Hebrew writes one `שָׁנָה` per numeral group where the ASV writes a single *years* — the rendered occurrence is the last, closing the whole Hebrew figure as the English noun closes the whole English one. Do not settle it by number agreement: Hebrew writes `שָׁנִים` after 2–10 and `שָׁנָה` from 11 up whatever the total, while the English plural follows the sum, so a match between them is an accident of two unrelated agreement systems and is not evidence. Do not settle it by which numeral the English noun stands beside either, since English drives the counted noun to the end of the phrase whatever order the translation chose. Tail-to-tail is what survives, and it holds across both Hebrew group orders and the ASV's frequent reordering of them. The genealogies are where this recurs, and BSB, which attaches the noun to its own phrase, disagrees on every first occurrence. **Tail-to-tail governs a run of absolute occurrences only.** Where the phrase is instead headed by a **construct** — a regnal date such as `בִּשְׁנַת עֶשְׂרִים וָשֶׁבַע שָׁנָה` → *In the twenty and seventh year* — the construct is what the English realizes, and the trailing absolute is the resumptive occurrence that goes `unrepresented`. So the rendered occurrence is the last of several absolutes but the first where a construct heads them, and MACULA's morphology is what decides which case this is. Position is the consequence, not the rule. **But a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a fused English word is not an unrendered occurrence.** Where a relative clause resumes its antecedent with a pronominal suffix on a preposition, or with a resumptive adverb, and the ASV writes one pronominal adverb for the whole — *wherein*, *whereon*, *whereby*, *whither*, and the bare *therein* of a preposition and its own suffix — the relative, the preposition and the resumptive morpheme share one unit under rule 30, headed on the relative, or on the preposition where no relative stands. Do not mark the suffix `unrepresented` under this rule's first sentence: rule 30's one-English-word condition is met, because that word carries the resumption as well as the relation, exactly as *Nor* carries both the coordination and the negation in rule 35. The corpus reads `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ` → *wherein* as one three-morpheme unit in twenty-one places and `בָּהּ` → *therein* as one two-morpheme unit in sixty-one, and records no unit where such a suffix stands outside the word. So ask first whether the English word carries the morpheme's sense: what this rule's first sentence governs is an element the ASV has left unwritten, as a second `בֵּין` or a surplus `שָׁנָה` is, and not one it has written inside a fusion. **A resumptive possessive suffix is read on exactly those terms, and it need not stand on a preposition.** Where the clause resumes its antecedent with a suffix on a noun inside it and the ASV writes one *whose* for the pair, the relative and that suffix share one unit under rule 30, headed on the relative, while the noun keeps its own English: `אֶרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אֲבָנֶיהָ בַרְזֶל` → *a land* ***whose*** *stones are iron* is one unit on `אֲשֶׁר` and the suffix, with *stones* left to `אֶבֶן`. Contiguity is not the condition, for the reason rule 35 gives: however much of the clause stands between them, the one English word still carries both the relation and the resumption, so nothing is left over to mark. The corpus reads `אֲשֶׁר` with its resumptive suffix as one *whose* unit at DEU.28.49 and 1KI.8.39, and as a `noncompositional` one at AMO.2.9 and DAN.10.1 among eighteen such places. **But read which morphemes stand in each clause before counting a second occurrence.** Where a further clause is coordinated under the one written relative and the ASV rewrites its *whose* at the head of that clause, a resumptive suffix standing in that clause is what the second word realizes, under rule 18's sentence giving a suffix the English relative pronoun that renders it: `וּמֵהֲרָרֶיהָ תַּחְצֹב נְחֹשֶׁת` → *and out of* ***whose*** *hills thou mayest dig copper* gives its *whose* to the suffix on `הֲרָרֶיהָ`, not to the relative as a repetition under rule 25. Where no such suffix stands in the coordinated clause, rule 55's distributed subordinator governs as before and every occurrence is the relative's.
amendments.why: DEU.8.9 read `אֲשֶׁר ... בָּהּ` → *wherein* as one unit and, five units later, marked the structurally identical resumptive suffix of `אֲשֶׁר אֲבָנֶיהָ בַרְזֶל` `unrepresented` beside a bare *whose*. Rule 22's existing fusion paragraph names only pronominal adverbs and only a suffix standing on a preposition, so a possessive resumption on a noun — and one held apart from the relative by that noun — fell through it and was disposed of by the rule's first sentence, which the same paragraph says it must not be. Amending rather than adding, so the over-broad first sentence is corrected where it stands: the corpus aligns `אֲשֶׁר` with its resumptive suffix to *whose* as one unit (DEU.28.49, 1KI.8.39, and eighteen `noncompositional` places including AMO.2.9 and DAN.10.1) and records none where the suffix stands outside the word, and BSB independently treats the DEU.8.9 suffix as represented. The closing sentences keep the coordinated-clause case from being read as licence to build a discontinuous relative unit over a clause that writes a resumptive morpheme of its own, which is rule 18's ruling and the one this chapter applied to DEU.8.9's second *whose*.

conventions: A relative clause resumed by a pronominal suffix and rendered by a single *whose* is one unit on the relative and that suffix, headed on the relative, exactly as `אֲשֶׁר ... בָּהּ` → *wherein* is (DEU.8.9, both). The suffix is not `unrepresented`, and the noun between them keeps its own English. Where a further clause is coordinated under the same written `אֲשֶׁר` and the ASV rewrites *whose*, that second word goes to the coordinated clause's own resumptive suffix under rule 18, not to the relative as a distributed repetition.

Supplied English subordinators in this chapter are counted against the conjunction morphemes standing in each clause, and the chapter writes both outcomes. Where a waw stands at the clause's left edge and the ASV writes coordinator and subordinator contiguously, the pair is one rendering of that waw and neither word is a surplus: *and when* (DEU.8.13), *and lest* (DEU.8.17, italic). Where the clause's only conjunction is `פֶּן`, which already holds its own *lest*, a further *when* is subordinator beside subordinator, no morpheme answers to it, and it is `added` (DEU.8.12). The same count leaves DEU.8.5's apodosis *so* `added` for want of any conjunction, while DEU.8.14's *then* goes to the waw written for it.

The ASV writes *fed thee with manna* twice from different Hebrew, and the two are deliberately aligned differently: DEU.8.3 has `אֵת` on `הַמָּן` and the marker takes the *with* (rule 16), while DEU.8.16 writes the object bare and the *with* joins the verb's unit (rule 44). Do not harmonise them; the present marker is what decides.

report: One real split, and it sits inside a single verse: DEU.8.9 fuses `אֲשֶׁר ... בָּהּ` into one three-morpheme *wherein* unit and then, five units later, marks the structurally identical resumptive suffix of `אֲשֶׁר אֲבָנֶיהָ בַרְזֶל` `unrepresented` beside a bare *whose*. Rule 22's closing paragraph forbids exactly that — the one English word carries the resumption as well as the relation — so `אֲשֶׁר` and the suffix now share one unit under rule 30, headed on the relative. Patched.

The second *whose* of DEU.8.9, in the coordinated clause where `אֲשֶׁר` is not rewritten, stays with that clause's own suffix on `הֲרָרֶיהָ` under rule 18; the competing reading (both *whose*s to `אֲשֶׁר` as a distributed repetition under rules 25 and 55, both suffixes unrepresented) is named in that unit's note.

Candidates checked and rejected as splits, each licensed by something written in the source. *fed thee with manna* twice: DEU.8.3 has `אֵת` on `הַמָּן` and the marker takes the *with* (rule 16), DEU.8.16 has no marker and the *with* joins the verb (rule 44) — rule 44's own limit says a present marker takes the word first. Subordinators: DEU.8.13 *and when* and DEU.8.17 *and lest* are one rendering of a waw standing at the clause's left edge (rules 55, 51), while DEU.8.12's *when* follows `פֶּן`, which already holds *lest*, so two subordinators answer to one conjunction and the surplus is `added`. Apodosis connectives: DEU.8.14's *then* has a waw for it, DEU.8.5's *so* has no conjunction morpheme at all and is `added` (rule 14).

Articles are read off the ASV verse by verse (rules 29, 41, 47) and every `הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה` phrase is counted the same way: the demonstrative pronoun takes the phrase's one determiner where one stands (8.17, 8.18), the article takes it where none does (8.1, 8.11, 8.19). `מִן` → *out of* heads on *out* in all four places (8.9, 8.14 twice, 8.15); `מֵעַל` (8.4) heads on the opening preposition and `מִפְּנֵי` (8.20) on the construct noun, which is rule 23's two clauses and not a disagreement.

BSB: no genuine error except DEU.8.9.018, the suffix just patched, where BSB is right that the morpheme is represented. The Sn ×8, Td ×9 and R ×7 blocks are the documented convention differences (rules 32, 29, 40). DEU.8.6 `אֹת` is rule 16; DEU.8.7 `בָ` is a second preposition the ASV does not rewrite; DEU.8.8 `שֶׁמֶן` is genuinely unrendered, since *olive trees* is spent on `זַיִת` and carries no *oil*, so rule 30's condition is unmet; DEU.8.19 `שָׁכֹחַ` is rule 56's last sentence, no adverbial word being written for it.

Left standing after review: DEU.8.11 `הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ` → *Beware*, where BSB represents the suffix. Rule 40's fusion paragraph was weighed and rejected because it turns on rule 30's condition, and *Beware* carries the verb's lexeme but not the ethical dative's own sense — the `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded* shape, where rule 2 splits and the preposition is `unrepresented`. The verse pass already named the competing fusion in the unit's note under rule 8, so this stays a documented tie rather than a correction.

Also left standing, each with the competing reading already named in its note: DEU.8.15 *wherein were* as one `added` unit (the Hebrew juxtaposes an appositional noun list with no clause in it, unlike the genuine verbless clause `אֲבָנֶיהָ בַרְזֶל` in 8.9, whose *are* goes to the predicate), DEU.8.18 `כְּ` → *as at*, and DEU.8.16 `אַחֲרִית` → *latter end* headed on *end*.
